title: Precision and the Burden of Proof
text:
In a formal argument, the precise meaning of a single term can decide whether a claim stands or falls. Philosophers distinguish between a necessary condition, which must be present for an outcome to occur, and a sufficient condition, which guarantees the outcome once it is present. Confusing the two is a common source of error, since a factor may be essential without being enough on its own to produce the conclusion.

Speakers who wish to avoid such confusion often qualify their claims with care. A statement that a treatment is 'likely to help' commits the speaker to less than one that it 'will cure', and the difference matters when evidence is limited. The burden of proof, in this sense, rests with whoever makes the stronger claim, because a weaker formulation is easier to defend against the objections of an opponent.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what is a necessary condition?
options: A factor that guarantees an outcome once it is present
A factor that must be present for an outcome to occur
A factor that always prevents an outcome
A factor that is irrelevant to the conclusion

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what does a statement that a treatment 'will cure' commit the speaker to?
options: Less than a statement that it is 'likely to help'
The same as a statement that it is 'likely to help'
Nothing at all about the treatment
More than a statement that it is 'likely to help'

questions.text: What does the passage imply about confusing necessary and sufficient conditions?
options: It is harmless when the factor is essential
It can lead to conclusions the evidence does not support
It is only a problem in mathematics

questions.text: Why might a weaker formulation be easier to defend?
options: Because it makes no claim that could be tested
Because it commits the speaker to less, so there is less to challenge
Because opponents always accept weak claims

vocabulary.definition: required in order for something to happen or be true
enough to achieve a result without needing anything further
to limit or modify a statement so that it is less absolute
reasons or arguments raised against a claim

paragraph_translations: W formalnym argumencie precyzyjne znaczenie jednego terminu może zadecydować o tym, czy twierdzenie się broni. Filozofowie odróżniają warunek konieczny, który musi być obecny, aby wynik mógł wystąpić, od warunku wystarczającego, który gwarantuje wynik, gdy już jest obecny. Pomylenie tych dwóch pojęć jest częstym źródłem błędów, ponieważ czynnik może być niezbędny, a mimo to niewystarczający sam w sobie, by doprowadzić do wniosku.

Mówcy, którzy chcą uniknąć takiej pomyłki, często starannie kwalifikują swoje twierdzenia. Stwierdzenie, że leczenie «prawdopodobnie pomoże», zobowiązuje mówcę do mniej niż stwierdzenie, że «wyleczy», a różnica ma znaczenie, gdy dowody są ograniczone. Ciężar dowodu spoczywa zatem na tym, kto formułuje mocniejsze twierdzenie, ponieważ słabsze sformułowanie łatwiej obronić przed zastrzeżeniami przeciwnika.
